Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

Redfin will highlight iconic American homes through the end of 2027. Know a home with a story worth telling? Nominate it for inclusion in the creative franchise using this form. Tour the first properties and get an alert when each new home debuts using redfin.com/iconic-homes.

Barcelona targeting January move for Tottenham Hotspur defender

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

Barnaby Lane is a highly experienced sports writer who has written for The Times, FourFourTwo Magazine, Sports Illustrated, TalkSPORT, and Business Insider. Over the years, he's had the pleasure of interviewing some of the biggest names in world sport, including Usain Bolt, Rafael Nadal, Christian Pulisic, and more.

Tottenham could face growing interest in one of their key players ahead of the January transfer window, with Barcelona president Joan Laporta reportedly keen on bringing Pedro Porro to the Nou Camp.

The Spanish right-back has attracted attention following his performances for Spain at the World Cup, but Spurs have several reasons to feel confident about keeping hold of the defender.

According to Catalan broadcaster 3Cat, Porro is one of Laporta’s preferred defensive targets as Barcelona consider whether to strengthen their backline in January.

The Catalan club have been dealing with a series of defensive injuries involving Eric Garcia, Jules Kounde, Andreas Christensen and Xavi Espart. However, Barcelona have not made a final decision on whether to bring in another defender, with the club waiting to assess the injured players’ recoveries.

Laporta’s admiration for Porro reportedly grew during Spain’s World Cup campaign. The Tottenham defender became an important part of the national team, developing a strong understanding with Lamine Yamal on the right flank and scoring twice during the tournament, including in the semi-final against France.

Laporta watched that semi-final in Dallas and was reportedly impressed by Porro’s performance. Barcelona had also gathered information about the defender towards the end of the previous summer transfer window, but their enquiry did not progress into a formal proposal to either the player or Tottenham.

Porro’s contractual situation gives Spurs a strong negotiating position. The 27-year-old renewed his contract shortly before the World Cup, committing his future to the north London club until 2031.

Reports have also indicated that Tottenham would demand a significant fee to consider allowing the defender to leave. Real Madrid have also been linked with an interest in the Spain international, potentially creating further competition for his signature.

Barcelona’s admiration for Porro is a reminder of the defender’s standing in European football, but there is currently no confirmed bid or formal approach.

Tottenham will be keen to retain a player who remains an important part of their plans. His long-term contract also means the club are under no immediate pressure to negotiate a sale.

The situation could develop if Barcelona decide their defensive injury problems require January reinforcements. For now, however, Spurs remain in a strong position, and any interested club would likely have to make a substantial offer to test their resolve.

Manchester City favourites to sign Borussia Dortmund star after formal approach

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

Barnaby Lane is a highly experienced sports writer who has written for The Times, FourFourTwo Magazine, Sports Illustrated, TalkSPORT, and Business Insider. Over the years, he's had the pleasure of interviewing some of the biggest names in world sport, including Usain Bolt, Rafael Nadal, Christian Pulisic, and more.

Manchester City are continuing to invest in young talent as they look to strengthen their squad for the future, with another exciting prospect emerging on their transfer radar.

Pep Guardiola’s side have reportedly moved into pole position for one of Borussia Dortmund’s most highly rated youngsters.

United States international Mathis Albert has attracted interest from several European clubs, but City are currently considered the favourites to secure his signature.

With the teenager’s first-team opportunities limited in Germany, the Premier League champions could look to take advantage of the situation.

According to TEAMtalk, Manchester City are the frontrunners to sign Albert after making a formal approach during the summer transfer window.

The report claims City are prepared to offer the 17-year-old lucrative personal terms as they step up their pursuit. Their interest is serious, with the club previously prepared to meet a valuation in the region of €20 million (£16.7m).

Chelsea are also long-term admirers of the youngster and were reportedly willing to spend a similar amount last winter. Paris Saint-Germain previously made contact with Dortmund in 2025, while Arsenal and Liverpool have more recently been monitoring his situation.

However, City are currently viewed as being in the strongest position should Dortmund soften their stance.

Albert joined Borussia Dortmund from the LA Galaxy academy in 2024 and has quickly established himself as one of the most exciting young American talents in European football. He has already made Bundesliga appearances and earned senior international recognition with the United States.

Despite his potential, opportunities under Niko Kovac have been limited this season. That lack of regular first-team football has encouraged several clubs to monitor his development, although Dortmund remain determined to keep hold of their young attacker.

The Bundesliga side have reportedly rejected approaches, including loan enquiries, and continue to view Albert as an important part of their long-term plans. They are also preparing a contract extension offer, with his current agreement running until June 2027.

There is another important factor for City. Premier League regulations prevent English clubs from signing Albert permanently until he turns 18 in May, meaning any potential transfer would be geared towards next summer rather than an immediate move.

Manchester United targeting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in surprise January transfer move

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

Barnaby Lane is a highly experienced sports writer who has written for The Times, FourFourTwo Magazine, Sports Illustrated, TalkSPORT, and Business Insider. Over the years, he's had the pleasure of interviewing some of the biggest names in world sport, including Usain Bolt, Rafael Nadal, Christian Pulisic, and more.

Manchester United could be forced to strengthen their attacking options in January after another injury setback involving Benjamin Sesko.

With Michael Carrick needing additional firepower to maintain competition for places up front, an experienced Premier League striker has reportedly emerged as a surprise target.

Leeds United forward Dominic Calvert-Lewin is among the names being considered by United’s recruitment team. However, attempting to sign a key player from one of their biggest rivals could prove extremely difficult.

According to The Athletic, Manchester United are exploring the January market for centre-forwards, with Calvert-Lewin one of the players under consideration.

The 29-year-old England international has reportedly been on United’s radar for some time, and recruitment staff are now assessing whether a potential transfer would be feasible when the window opens.

The interest comes amid concerns over Benjamin Sesko’s availability. The Slovenian striker is expected to miss an extended period with a shin injury, leaving Carrick with fewer recognised centre-forward options.

Calvert-Lewin has rebuilt his career since joining Leeds on a free transfer from Everton in 2025. His performances at Elland Road have attracted renewed attention, with the striker scoring 20 goals in 49 appearances for the club across all competitions.

He has also returned to England international contention following his improved form, making him an appealing option for United as they consider their attacking requirements.

However, there are significant obstacles. Leeds are reportedly keen to reward Calvert-Lewin with a new contract, despite his current agreement running until 2028. The club are also understood to be protective of a player who has become an important part of Daniel Farke’s side.

The rivalry between Leeds and Manchester United presents another major complication. A transfer between the clubs would attract considerable attention, and reports suggest the possibility of an agreement is currently remote.

Calvert-Lewin could offer United a different profile in attack, bringing physical presence, aerial ability and considerable Premier League experience. His availability could become particularly important if Sesko remains sidelined into the January window.

United have previously considered alternative centre-forward options, but the latest developments could encourage the recruitment department to widen its search. Calvert-Lewin’s experience in English football would potentially make him an attractive short-term solution.

Nevertheless, Leeds are unlikely to make negotiations straightforward. They have little reason to weaken their squad midway through the campaign, particularly by allowing an important player to join their historic rivals.

United must also consider whether pursuing Calvert-Lewin is realistic when other striker targets may be easier to acquire.

For now, the reported interest represents an option under consideration rather than an imminent transfer. Sesko’s injury has increased the urgency surrounding United’s search for attacking reinforcements, but persuading Leeds to sell their striker could prove a significant challenge.

Former U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information and Stealing Night Vision Goggles

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

Ashbacher was charged by an indictment unsealed Tuesday with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and with theft of government property.

According to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private company that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

Trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

The Buried Tamales at the Heart of the Yucatán’s Day of the Dead

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

On a fall afternoon in Halachó, a small town in the Mexican state of Yucatán, Wilson Alonzo stood before a smoldering mound of dirt and began digging. Slowly clearing away branches, leaves, and soil, the chef unearthed a large disc enclosed in banana leaves. He peeled the wrapping back and examined the golden edges of the round tamale inside. He nodded. It was ready for the altar.

Every October and November, Yucatecans like Alonzo gather at the edges of underground ovens and cook mukbil pollo (“buried chicken”), a sacred tamale made only for the Yucatán Peninsula’s Day of the Dead. Known as Janal Pixán (“Food for the Souls” in Yucatec Maya) or Los Finados, the holiday welcomes returning spirits: children on October 31, adults on November 1, and all spirits on November 2, followed by a farewell feast eight—or in some cases, 30—days later. Above anything else that might grace an ofrenda, which could include anything from hot chocolate to relleno negro to beer, mukbil pollo is the star that occupies every altar’s center.

“It is the absolute highlight of the offering,” Alonzo said. One bite confirms why: The crispy, caramelized crust of lard-enriched masa gives way to a smoky, savory mouthful of chicken bathed in a brothy crimson sauce of achiote, tomato, sweet and spicy peppers, epazote, onions, and garlic.

But Alonzo—whose restaurant, Ya’axche, specializes in traditional Yucatecan dishes—said it’s not mukbil pollo’s flavor that nourishes spirits; instead of eating it, they consume the tamale through its aroma. And a crucial part of that aroma, he added, comes from the píib. Dating back to the ancient Maya, this underground cooking technique uses wood, stones, and leaves to impart a slightly herbaceous, smoky succulence to dishes like mukbil pollo—also known as pibipollo or pib—and cochinita pibil.“Cooking it in a gas oven simply isn’t the same,” Alonzo said. “You lose the unique aromas and flavors imparted by the earth itself.”Not everyone sees the píib as essential. In cities, where outdoor space is limited, most tamales are baked indoors. When Steffan Igor Ayora-Díaz, a retired anthropologist, was growing up in the city of Valladolid, his mother made mukbil pollo at home, then brought it to a local bakery to cook in an industrial oven. “Nobody said, ‘Oh, it has to be in a píib,’ ” he explained.

Ayora-Díaz now lives in the Yucatán state capital of Mérida, where he said beliefs surrounding Janal Pixán lean more secular. Not only do most eschew the píib, but he and many of his friends no longer build ofrendas, instead celebrating the holiday by gathering with family over a meal. Mukbil pollo is still important, but it plays a role more analogous to turkey on Thanksgiving. “We’re still going to eat it because that’s the food that you eat on these days, but you’re not really thinking of dead people when you’re eating it,” he said.

While purists decry these nontraditional approaches to the holiday, Ayora-Díaz points out that mukbil pollo is a blend of ancient and modern. “It’s a ‘traditional’ dish, but I’m putting ‘traditional’ in quotes because it’s relatively new,” he said. The Maya have been cooking in píibs and eating tamales for millennia, but ingredients like garlic, onions, and lard arrived with the Spanish conquistadors in the 1500s. And, according to Ayora-Díaz, mukbil pollo only started appearing in written records in the 1900s.Janal Pixán, too, is a hybrid of sorts, blending Christian rituals for All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day with Maya beliefs surrounding death and ancestor veneration. In Xocén, a small village of largely Yucatec Maya residents about 20 minutes outside Valladolid, honoring the dead can mean not only praying for their souls at Catholic mass but welcoming them into one’s home as guests and offering them the same hospitality as the living.

“We are dealing with spirits who require respect and specific observances, and who actually come to visit us,” Miguel Tun, a Yucatec Maya tour guide, said. “Even the yards look clean during this time. You walk past someone’s house and see that everything is spotless because visitors are coming.”Tun lives in a modern home next to his parents’ palapa in Xocén. The Tuns, like many Yucatec Maya, make their tamales only for the biix, or eighth day of Janal Pixán, when souls are believed to return to purgatory. In Xocén, the local version of mukbil pollo is perfectly suited for this journey. Called chachak waaj (“red tamale” in Yucatec Maya), it’s like a small hand pie.

“The idea is that the souls can easily carry the food with them,” Tun said. “It’s about seeing them off. It’s like when people travel—say, from abroad—to visit, and we give them a gift.”

This gift isn’t just the tamale itself but the time spent creating it. I visited the Tuns to learn how to make chachak waaj from scratch. We began in the morning. After shredding chicken, slow-cooking sauce, mixing manteca (rendered pork lard) into masa, assembling each tamale, and wrapping them in banana leaves, we needed headlamps to navigate the píib in the darkness.

“If you are going to make an offering as part of a spiritual practice, it has to be something into which you have poured your effort, you have sacrificed your time,” he said. “That holds significant meaning within the Maya worldview.”

The hours spent making chachak waaj also provide an opportunity to reminisce about the dead. “It’s a moment where the whole family is together, remembering things while cooking, making preparations, or kneading the dough,” Tun said. “Sometimes the conversation is about what’s happening in the community, but there are moments where someone makes a comment about something the deceased person used to do or say.”

At 9:30 p.m., Tun and his father returned from the backyard píib carrying several trays of tamales. It was time for the final step. The Tuns, several cousins, and an aunt gathered on plastic chairs and tree stumps and started unwrapping. They inspected each crust, making sure it was sufficiently crispy (the ones that weren’t would head back to the píib). As they worked, scattering charred leaves at their feet, they talked about an upcoming dance recital for one of their cousins.Later Tun told me this is, for him, the most important part of Janal Pixán. “Even though a loved one is gone, you demonstrate strength, you show that the family remains united,” he said. “You want that person, when they arrive, to see everyone together, to see that bond. That’s what matters most. I believe that’s the true essence of the Day of the Dead.”

The Tuns, like many Yucatec Maya, make their tamales only for the biix, or eighth day of Janal Pixán, when souls are believed to return to purgatory. In Xocén, the local version of mukbil pollo is perfectly suited for this journey. Called chachak waaj (“red tamale” in Yucatec Maya), it’s like a small hand pie.

“The idea is that the souls can easily carry the food with them,” Tun said. “It’s about seeing them off. It’s like when people travel—say, from abroad—to visit, and we give them a gift.”

This gift isn’t just the tamale itself but the time spent creating it. I visited the Tuns to learn how to make chachak waaj from scratch. We began in the morning. After shredding chicken, slow-cooking sauce, mixing manteca (rendered pork lard) into masa, assembling each tamale, and wrapping them in banana leaves, we needed headlamps to navigate the píib in the darkness.

“If you are going to make an offering as part of a spiritual practice, it has to be something into which you have poured your effort, you have sacrificed your time,” he said. “That holds significant meaning within the Maya worldview.”

The hours spent making chachak waaj also provide an opportunity to reminisce about the dead. “It’s a moment where the whole family is together, remembering things while cooking, making preparations, or kneading the dough,” Tun said. “Sometimes the conversation is about what’s happening in the community, but there are moments where someone makes a comment about something the deceased person used to do or say.”

At 9:30 p.m., Tun and his father returned from the backyard píib carrying several trays of tamales. It was time for the final step. The Tuns, several cousins, and an aunt gathered on plastic chairs and tree stumps and started unwrapping. They inspected each crust, making sure it was sufficiently crispy (the ones that weren’t would head back to the píib). As they worked, scattering charred leaves at their feet, they talked about an upcoming dance recital for one of their cousins.Later Tun told me this is, for him, the most important part of Janal Pixán. “Even though a loved one is gone, you demonstrate strength, you show that the family remains united,” he said. “You want that person, when they arrive, to see everyone together, to see that bond. That’s what matters most. I believe that’s the true essence of the Day of the Dead.”

This week featured a robust lineup of large rounds, led by manufacturing startup Re:Build, which closed on $2.1 billion, and predictions marketplace Kalshi, which picked up another $1 billion. Other sectors in which startups drew significant rounds included construction automation, biotech, batteries and enterprise AI.

1. Re:Build, $2.1B, manufacturing: Re:Build, a manufacturing startup that partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production, secured $2.1 billion in new funding. General Catalyst and JPMorganChase led the financing for the 6-year-old, Framingham, Massachusetts-based company.

2. Kalshi, $1B, predictions marketplace: Predictions marketplace Kalshi announced a $1 billion Series G financing led by Wellington Management and Sequoia Capital. The round set a $40 billion post-money valuation for New York-based Kalshi, which says its business’ annualized trading volume now exceeds $1 trillion.

3. Bedrock Robotics, $600M, construction tech: San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics,  a developer of autonomous systems for heavy equipment used in construction, raised $600 million in Series C funding led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital. The round brings Bedrock’s total funding to nearly $1 billion and sets a post-money valuation of $4.1 billion.

4. Dren Bio, $350M, biotech: Dren Bio, a developer of antibody therapeutics for cancer and autoimmune diseases, closed on $350 million in a new round led by Juvia Group and Lightspeed Venture Partners. The funding will support advanced trials for the San Carlos, California-based company’s blood cancer therapies.

5. Group 14 Technologies, $169M, battery tech: Woodinville, Washington-based Group 14 Technologies, a manufacturer and supplier of advanced silicon battery materials, picked up $169 million in Series D extension funding. The company also announced plans to expand into Europe with a production facility in Sagunto, Spain.

6. (tied) Firehawk Aerospace, $150M, defense tech: Firehawk Aerospace, a developer of propulsion technology, said it secured over $150 million in Series D funding at a valuation of more than $1.4 billion. Advent and Rochefort led the financing for the 7-year-old, Dallas-based company.

6. (tied) Serval, $150M, enterprise AI: Serval, a startup focused on coding agents for enterprise automation, raised $150 million in Series C funding at a $3 billion valuation. Sequoia Capital led the round for the 2-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

8. (tied) General Compute, $100M, AI infrastructure: AI cloud provider General Compute picked up $100 million in Series A funding led by Blackbird and Abstract. The company is building out its infrastructure using inference chips from Nvidia rivals Cerebras Systems, SambaNova and Positron AI.

8. (tied) Foundry Robotics, $100M, autonomous factories: Emeryville, California-based Foundry Robotics, a startup focused on building and operating autonomous factories, closed on $100 million in a Series A funding round led by Marlinspike.

8(tied) Hex Technologies, $100M, data analytics: Hex Technologies, a startup focused on building an AI-native platform for data analytics, secured $100 million in new financing. Peak XV and 137 Ventures led the round, which set a $1.2 billion valuation for the San Francisco-based company.

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Oct. 24-30, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

A Conversation Between Alex Honnold and Jim Morrison on ‘Everest: The Other Side’

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

At first glance, it might not seem like Alex Honnold’s free solo of El Capitan has much in common with Jim Morrison’s first ski descent of Everest’s north face, which is documented in Jimmy Chin’s new film Everest: The Other Side, which releases today, October 30.

But in a conversation during a live recording of Climbing Gold in May, it became clear that several parallels exist between these historic firsts:

Despite their shared sky-high risk tolerance, both Honnold and Morrison also agree with the general public on one thing: They consider each other “crazy.” Morrison called Honnold’s ropeless ascent of El Cap “totally insane.” Meanwhile, Honnold struggled to identify the line one might ski down Everest’s north side in a photo. Once Morrison pointed it out, Honnold declared: “That seems like death.”

The Hornbein Couloir on the northern Tibet side of Everest has taken the lives of several climbers, including the snowboarder Marco Siffredi who attempted to make the first descent of the couloir in 2002; his body has never been found.

Two Americans, Thomas Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, made the first ascent of Everest’s north side in 1963. The north side’s first ascent came just 22 days after Jim Whittaker became the first American to climb Everest via the south side. The 9,000-foot couloir they took to the top was colloquially known as “Hornbein’s Avalanche Chute.” Jimmy Chin also attempted an ascent of Hornbein’s in 2003, but was caught in a near-deadly avalanche.

At the age of 50, after two failed attempts and the staggering loss of Hilaree Nelson, his partner in life and mountains, on Manaslu, Morrison skied down Hornbein’s Couloir on October 15. He pulled it off just four months after undergoing a partial knee replacement. Before Morrison’s ascent last fall—which included a 12-person team of Sherpas, Ecuadorian fixers, and filmmakers—no human had successfully ascended the line since 1991.

Honnold’s conversation with Morrison about his historic ski descent was part of the first-ever live recording of Fitz Cahall’s and Honnold’s Climbing Gold podcast. The interview took the stage at Outside Days on May 31 in Denver, CO. The podcast episode dropped today, alongside the release of the film. You can watch an excerpt above, and read on for Honnold’s and Morrison’s thoughts on grief, the question they dread most, and risking their lives for sport.

Morrison conceived of the goal to ski down Everest’s Hornbein Couloir with Hilaree Nelson. The two ski mountaineers met on Makalu (8,463m) in 2015 and fell in love.

“We were on a tear,” Morrison told Honnold and Cahall, “ticking off these dream runs all over the planet.”

The two had been trying to get to Everest to attempt their ski descent. But COVID delayed their plans, making it impossible to get to the Chinese side of the mountain. To stay in 8,000-meter-peak shape, in 2022, they headed to Manaslu (8,163m) where Morrison recalls they “had a pretty incredible day all by ourselves up on the mountain.” He started skiing down first; Nelson followed, but when Morrison stopped to wait for her, she never appeared. She had set off a small avalanche. “What ensued was a multi-day, horrific rescue of her and trying to find her,” he said. “And it changed my life.”

At first, Morrison wanted to hang it up—never ski or head into the mountains again. But eventually, he began to realize “this is part of me, this is in me.” And he returned to the goal they’d started together. “I wanted to do it for her, and her legacy, and us.”

On the summit, Morrison spread some of Nelson’s ashes. “It was a really emotional moment for me, looking off at mountains I had skied with her, Lhotse and Makalu,” he reflected. “I really felt like she was there.”

In 2011, before losing Nelson on Manaslu, Morrison’s wife, daughter, and son passed away in a plane crash. While he has experienced unfathomable loss, he continues to try to push past the grief to keep living. On stage, he shared a metaphor he uses to grapple with loss:

I’ve described grief as a big heavy wet blanket that gets put on you. It’s just really hard. You go through a process of losing a loved one or spouse or child and it’s a really heavy weight. I like to think over time you take that blanket and you dry it out and you begin to fold it up. And eventually, you put it in a backpack and you carry it with you.

After free soloing El Cap, Honnold said his life became “a crazy whirlwind.” A week and a half later, he was on an expedition in Alaska. Then the film came out, thus marking his “six month deployment to Hollywood” of screenings and award ceremonies.

The effect was that his memories of free soloing El Cap blurred with the scenes from the film as he watched himself on the big screen, again and again. What he’d set out to do for himself became a messy, public experience. As Chin releases his film, Morrison may undergo a similar experience of distorted memories and mayhem.

Honnold also recalled the dreaded question punted at him on his Hollywood deployment: What’s next?

Morrison received the same question after his Everest descent and gave an answer Honnold wished he’d come up with years ago: Isn’t this enough?

“I just achieved this 10-year life dream,” Honnold joked of receiving the “what’s next” question. “I don’t have another life dream lined up on the back burner.”

Morrison called achieving his Everest ski descent goal an “incredible journey” and noted that he appreciated the team that supported him throughout the process.

Cahall teed up his last question by warning that “some of this is triggering to some people.” Meaning, this talk of visualizing fatal falls, of risking it all for the goal. But, Cahall wondered: Are we mistaking complacency for safety?

Morrison said that he doesn’t really see it as complacency versus risk. It’s not an either/or situation. “This is what I’m drawn to and this is what my life’s goals have been centered around,” he said. “I’m not going out there to make a mistake and not come home.” He added that while his ski descent might seem like a “horrendously risky thing,” it was the culmination of extensive planning and preparation, just like Honnold’s El Cap free solo.

“It’s really hard to look at you climbing El Cap without a rope and rationalize it and understand it and be able to relate to it because it is so totally insane,” Morrison said. But at the same time, he said he held “deep respect” for all of the preparation and focus Honnold put into ticking the goal.

“Without taking some amount of personal risk, you just can’t lead a rich and fulfilled life,” Honnold added. “People watch the film Free Solo or a film like that and they’re like, ‘Well, that’s crazy!’ Yeah it’s unusual, not the sort of risk taking you normally see, but it’s still making smart choices in their life in order to lead the most fulfilled life that they can.”

Athletic Club academy trio score first senior goals in 6-1 Copa del Rey win at Prat

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

Three academy players scored their first goals for Athletic Club's senior side inside four minutes as Edin Terzić's team beat Prat 6-1 in the Copa del Rey. The late burst came from substitutes in a side rotated with the Basque derby in mind.

On Thursday 29 October, Athletic met Prat in the Copa del Rey round of 128. The tie was played at the Estadi La Feixa Llarga in L’Hospitalet de Llobregat. Its closing stages belonged to Athletic’s academy.

Each of the late scorers had come off the bench. Selton Sánchez finished the night with the sixth goal, teed up by Vizcay, whose own strike had started the flurry.

Aritz Conde earned an 8.2 rating from the data provider for his half-hour on the pitch. Imga, aged just 17, had made his first-team debut alongside Vizcay against Getafe the previous Sunday.

EFE reported that Athletic picked a starting XI shaped by the coming Basque derby, giving chances to players such as Yohaneko, Sannadi and Nico Serrano. Those changes did not slow the visitors.

Maroan Sannadi opened the scoring in the 29th minute. Robert Navarro doubled the lead two minutes later. Mikel Jauregizar provided both assists. Gustavo Reinke pulled one back for Prat in the 33rd minute, set up by Álex Plaza. Serrano restored the two-goal cushion three minutes later from a Jesús Areso pass.

The statistics show how one-sided the night was. Athletic had 68% of the ball and 20 shots from inside the box. They put 12 attempts on target, against 2 from the hosts. Prat’s goalkeeper was kept busy with six saves. Navarro earned the top rating of 9.2, with seven key passes in 86 minutes.

Miguel Ángel Motoso’s Prat came into the tie after beating San Rafael 5-1 and 5-0 in their two previous matches. The draw carried an echo for Athletic. Their run to their most recent Copa title began on 1 November 2023 against another Liga Élite Catalana side, about 22 km from L’Hospitalet.

The Lions are through to the next round after an excellent performance against @aeprat1945

👏 Great work, lads!#AEPratAthletic 🏆 #AthleticClub 🦁 pic.twitter.com/BLfqr4bwpf

— Athletic Club (@Athletic_en) October 29, 2026

The rotation leaves Terzić’s regular attackers fresher for the weekend. On Sunday 1 November, San Mamés stages the LaLiga matchday 11 meeting with Real Sociedad, kicking off at 21:00 Spanish time. Athletic’s recent results include a 1-0 win over the same opponents.

The cup run now pauses. The RFEF’s first national round brought in 112 of the 116 clubs entered in this season’s competition, which runs until 24 April 2027. The last 32 is set for 16 December, with the last 16 on 6 January. Before that, the second round is scheduled for 2 December.

Halloween in the Garden: 3 Spooky and Creative Displays

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

Happy Friday, GPOD! Halloween is tomorrow, so for our last post of the week, I couldn’t resist digging through past GPODs for a little spooky-season garden inspiration. Over the years, contributors have shown us that Halloween decor doesn’t have to stop at the front door. A foggy morning can turn a familiar garden wonderfully eerie, homegrown pumpkins can become an entire cast of characters, and flowers and foliage from the garden can transform simple gourds into works of art. Today we’re revisiting three very different Halloween displays that all have their own charm and appeal.

We’ll start in Hebron, Kentucky, with Keri Shinault’s perfectly spooky garden. Keri and her husband, Brandon, began hosting an annual Halloween masquerade after their October 2005 wedding, eventually decorating their home and garden with creepy critters, ghouls, headstones, and plenty of other spooky surprises.

A beautiful sitting area surrounded by lush plants becomes instantly more mysterious when fog blurs the garden beyond.

Sometimes Mother Nature provides the best Halloween special effects.

Sit a while! Take a load off those tired bones.

Stepping stones set into lush ground covers guide you around massive oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia, Zones 5–9) shrubs.

Next up are Tom and Jeannie Tremont’s delightfully ridiculous pumpkin people. Rather than simply lining the porch with gourds, Tom and Jeannie turned their pumpkins into an entire cast of characters with their own poses, props, and personalities.

Why settle for a jack-o’-lantern when your pumpkins can go for a bike ride? Tom and Jeannie turned their fall harvest into a whole cast of characters, complete with wheels.

Tom and Jeannie Tremont clearly weren’t interested in ordinary jack-o’-lanterns. This pumpkin person looks like they got caught with their pants down while a family bikes by in the background. It’s ridiculous in the best possible way.

The mama-and-baby pumpkin pair might be the sweetest of the bunch. Even commenters on the original GPOD singled this little duo out as a favorite.

We’ll end with something completely different from Cherry Ong in Richmond, British Columbia. For her dazzling pumpkin display, Cherry repurposed the pallet-wood auricula theaters she and her husband had built for spring into a stage for decorated pumpkins and squash.

Auricula theaters traditionally protect auriculas (Primula auricula, Zones 3–8) from harsh rain and wind, but Cherry discovered they make a pretty spectacular fall display too.

Cherry and her husband built these pallet-wood auricula theaters a couple of years earlier—he constructed and hung the boxes, while Cherry designed and stained them. In fall, the shelves get a totally new look when pumpkins and gourds take the place of spring flowers.

Cherry had a little fun displaying the smaller pumpkins before giving them away, using old mini terra-cotta pots to add height and variation. Some pumpkins were decorated with seasonal flowers and foliage from the garden, turning the whole theater into one big botanical arrangement.

A small white pumpkin topped with clusters of Chinese tea rosebuds shows just how detailed Cherry gets with these creations. Elsewhere in the display, she also incorporated dried dahlias and other flowers and foliage from the garden.

I love how each of these gardeners found a unique way to bring Halloween into their outdoor spaces. That might be my favorite thing about Halloween in the garden: there really aren’t many rules. You can go creepy, silly, beautiful, botanical—or somehow all four at once. I hope everyone has a happy Halloween tomorrow! If you’re decorating your garden, porch, containers, or homegrown pumpkins this weekend, I’d love to see what you come up with.

How ADHD Science Fails Women in Menopause

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

Menopause worsens ADHD symptoms, but standard assessments do not capture the depth of women’s misery.

Menopause aggravates and elevates ADHD symptoms for a staggering 97.5 percent of women with the condition, according to a survey of 600 women cited in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.1 Complaints include increased difficulty with attention, emotional regulation, and managing everyday demands – symptoms that significantly degrade quality of life yet remain largely unaddressed in midlife ADHD treatment plans.

The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) – one of the standard measures for assessing common ADHD symptoms – may not fully capture how much menopause interferes with daily life because it was not specifically designed to measure changes in ADHD across hormonal transitions.

While nearly all of the 600 women in the survey reported worsening ADHD symptoms during menopause, their ASRS scores were similar across different hormonal life stages. This apparent contradiction deserves attention. A woman may experience a major change in mental clarity, working memory, motivation, emotional regulation, and managing day-to-day responsibilities without necessarily showing a large change on a standard ADHD symptom checklist.

[Get This Free Download: Menopause and ADHD]

This points to a critical need for better ways to assess ADHD across the lifespan and to understand how hormonal changes may alter its presentation and impact.

Today, we know about ADHD in menopause thanks, largely, to women’s personal accounts. Though surveys and self-reports cannot establish cause and effect in the same way as controlled clinical trials, they are an essential starting point. They can identify patterns and raise questions that researchers need to investigate.

One central question is regarding the safety and efficacy of prescribing hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and/or ADHD medication to women in perimenopause and menopause. Sadly, evidence specifically supporting combined HRT and stimulant treatment remains limited. We need well-designed studies to determine which women might benefit, what treatments are most effective, and how the medications may interact.

[Read: How Hormonal Changes Impact ADHD Symptoms in Women]

The voices of women with ADHD have brought this issue into view. Now clinicians and researchers have an opportunity – and a responsibility – to listen carefully, investigate rigorously, and translate emerging knowledge into better care.

Kathleen Nadeau, Ph.D., is the founder and clinical director of the Institute for Lifespan ADHD Training.

Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF

Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.

Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.

There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”

He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.

“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective

Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.

South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.

Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.

The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.

However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.

“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.

“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

Google’s Collapse Gives Hope for the Middle Class and Our Kids

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

I’ve been a Google shareholder since 2010 and I'm thankful. But yesterday’s earnings, and the 12% collapse that followed, left me thoroughly disappointed.

Search is under siege. Gemini isn’t leading the AI race. And Google is spending like a drunken sailor to catch up.

Spending $200 billion in CAPEX is more than the GDP of most countries. And free cash flow just went negative $9 billion for the quarter.

What does $200 billion buy you? Third or fourth place in the AI race, depending on who you ask. Behind Anthropic. Behind OpenAI. Maybe neck and neck with whoever else is closing fast.

That’s pathetic. And as a shareholder, it’s demoralizing. Not even Berkshire Hathaway investing $10 billion at $350/share can save us.

Google researchers wrote the 2017 paper that introduced the transformer, the “T” in ChatGPT. Google owns DeepMind. It designs its own TPU chips. It has Search, YouTube, Android, Gmail, and roughly 3 billion Chrome users. It understood large language models years before most of us knew what it was.

And yet most developers aren’t coding with Gemini. They’re using Claude Code, Codex, or something else.

In the most transformational technology since the internet went mainstream, Google had a ten-mile head start, outspent nearly everyone, and still got lapped.

Meanwhile, executives collected enormous pay packages. Nice work, which most of us can't get.

Everybody in the Bay Area knows Google is one of the best places to “rest and vest.” HBO’s Silicon Valley spoofed it with Big Head, who got promoted at Hooli into a big title, a rooftop office, and zero responsibilities.

Who doesn’t want to get paid a lot to work less? Of course there are plenty of hard-working people at Google.

But resting and vesting only feels good when the stock keeps going up. When the stock stalls, you’re just resting and asking whether this is all there is to life.

I’ve seen this movie before. I left Credit Suisse in 2012 partly because technology was squeezing the business. Algorithmic trading was compressing commissions toward zero, which is why trading is basically free today.

Our Asian equities group was competitive. But the firm overall was lagging Goldman, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, and UBS. Staying at a firm falling behind, in an industry being hollowed out, felt like polishing brass on a sinking ship.

So I left to build my own thing. I made a fraction of my old income for years. But watching something I built actually grow was more thrilling than any bonus check.

Momentum is energizing. Decline is a slow poison, even when the paycheck clears.

Part of the reason I invested in Google was its dominance. Two Stanford PhD students, who fittingly never finished their PhDs, hired an army of brilliant nerds from Stanford, MIT, and the Indian Institute of Technology.

They commanded over 90% search market share. They piled up over $100 billion in cash. Then they used monopoly profits to enter new businesses and crush the competition.

In other words, Google became the trust fund kid. Let’s call him Chip.

Chip was born on third base. Parent's money, the search monopoly, pays for everything. Grandpa’s name is on the library, which is the transformer paper and DeepMind. Family friends can make one phone call and open any door, which is Android, Chrome, and the default search deal with Apple.

Chip still posts on Instagram about his “grind” while sipping a $28 smoothie.

Everybody else in the AI race is the middle-class or poor kid. There is no way Chip should lose his incredible head start, unless he really messes up.

OK, maybe I’m being a little extreme. OpenAI has Microsoft’s money. Anthropic has Amazon’s money. Their founders went to Princeton, Stanford, and other elite schools. Nobody here is eating ramen.

But wealth is relative. If everybody is a millionaire, nobody is rich. Next to Google, everybody is middle class.

Google started the AI race with billions of users, a cash machine, and its own chips. Everyone else started with zero users and had to beg investors for money just to rent compute. Every dollar they raised came with a pitch deck and a deadline.

The middle-class kid has to justify every dollar. The trust fund kid just asks Dad for $200 billion.

And here’s the most trust fund kid thing of all. Google is an investor in Anthropic. Chip is literally paying tuition for the kid who’s beating him.

As a capitalist, you usually don’t bet against Chip when he’s smart and connected. You invest in him. I’ve watched the kid with every advantage win since 2004, when Google went public.

But every so often, Chip gets comfortable. He takes a third gap year. He hires expensive consultants to tell him what he should already know. Shiny object syndrome takes hold, and financial resources and attention get diverted to solving core problems.

Meanwhile, the middle-class kid has no safety net. If he doesn’t ship, he doesn’t eat.

Dario Amodei is a good example. He grew up middle class in San Francisco. His dad was a leather craftsman. His mom managed library projects. He went to Lowell, a public high school, studied hard, and actually finished his PhD.

In 2021, he co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela and a group of colleagues. Five years later, Claude is what developers reach for, and Anthropic is one of the most valuable private companies on earth.

It’s Google versus the world. And the world is the rest of us.

The trust fund kid has every advantage except one. He doesn’t need to win.

The middle-class kid has only one advantage. He must win or be relegated to the permanent underclass.

Hunger is the great equalizer. And unlike a trust fund, it can’t be inherited.

There’s another reason I’m not shedding too many tears for Chip, even though my portfolio needs to go to the ER. For years, he’s been taking other people’s lunch money.

Google built its empire by sending traffic to websites like mine. That was the deal. Bloggers, journalists, and small publishers created the content. Google organized it, sold ads around it, and sent readers our way. Everybody ate.

First came featured snippets, which lifted our answers onto the results page so readers didn’t need to click. Then Google stuffed its own products at the top: shopping results, travel results, maps, “People also ask” boxes, and more ads. The organic results, the content people actually searched for, got pushed so far down you needed a scuba tank to find them.

Then came AI Overviews. Now Google reads our work, summarizes it, and serves it as its own answer at the top of the page. The attribution, if there is any, is a tiny link most people never click.

Imagine writing from firsthand experience since 2009, only to watch a multi-trillion-dollar company repackage your insights and keep the reader. That’s not a search engine. That’s a very polite pickpocket.

And yes, I know the AI companies trained on publishers’ work too without attribution or payment. You have to steal people’s work to get rich sometimes. Nobody in this race has clean hands. But Google was supposed to be the partner. It sent us traffic for two decades before deciding it would rather keep it. So now it stomps on us too.

I don’t want to oversell the hope. Since graduating college in 1999, I’ve watched the rich get far richer than everybody else.

The first reason is math. The rich have more capital, so a bull market hands them bigger absolute dollar gains. The longer compounding runs, the bigger the pile gets.

I saw it at Goldman in NYC, at Credit Suisse in SF, and every year since I left in 2012. Some friends from my tennis club who were mere millionaires 15 years ago are now multi-billionaires.

The second reason is proximity. Rich people mostly hang out with other rich people. And proximity creates opportunity.

Once you’re an LP, you might get invited to co-invest in a hot private AI company the fund has high conviction in. That’s how the gap widens, one quiet invitation at a time. Be nice and helpful to as many people as possible.

Everybody rolls their eyes at networking. I hated it too. It’s likely the main reason I never made Managing Director. I couldn’t fake enough agreeableness with the powers that be.

The lesson to pass to our kids: you don’t have to be fake. But you do have to show up and always play nice with others if you want to get ahead

The beauty of FIRE is freedom. The problem with being a FIRE parent is that your network withers once you leave the workforce.

The people who could introduce you to clients, write a preschool recommendation letter, or refer you for a better job slowly disappear. And if you’re truly FIRE, you stop caring about getting ahead. Otherwise you’d still be trading time for money.

Then you have kids. And suddenly, money and status matter again in a hurry.

That’s why Google’s stumble actually provides hope, despite the paper loss.

If a company with $100 billion in cash, 3 billion users, the transformer itself, and a $200 billion annual budget can fumble its lead, then advantages aren’t destiny. They’re a head start. And head starts can be squandered.

Which means a hungry kid with no connections still has a real shot. So does the poorest minority kid in America.

My children won’t inherit a monopoly. But they can inherit a work ethic, some hunger, and the knowledge that Chip can be beaten.

Look, you’ve had a great run. Thank you for your hard work all these years. Google’s strategic drift isn’t your fault. That’s on the C-suite.

But as a shareholder, I have two requests.

This is wartime, not peacetime. Mass layoffs are likely coming, and the people who survive them tend to be the ones who are visibly in the building.

It’s been fun playing pickleball with many of you at 11:30 a.m. on a Tuesday. I’ll miss the competition. But that has to stop now.

The stock could be dead money for a year or two while the supertanker turns. If you’re only staying for the next vest, you’re not resting. You’re rotting.

Golden handcuffs are still handcuffs. And gold is heavy.

Go be the middle-class kid again in your own career. Join or start something where you have to win. That’s what Jeff Dean and colleagues did with the launch of Discovery Loop.

What doesn’t work is the middle path: staying, coasting, and feeling empty. That’s the worst of both worlds for you and for us shareholders. If you decide to leave, please try to negotiate a severance package. You have nothing to lose.

Google has the resources to recover. Trust fund kids usually get a second or third chance. The only question is whether Chip still wants it badly enough. It’s hard when you’re already so rich.

Readers, do you think Google can regain its AI lead, or has the trust fund kid permanently lost his edge? Is spending $200 billion a year a sign of strength or desperation? If you work at a big tech company, are you resting and vesting, or quietly planning your exit? And as a parent, how are you teaching your kids to compete without a trust fund or a powerful network?

100% disagree! As someone working inside Google Cloud after spending 6 years at AWS, I see a very different reality than the doomsday narrative around Google’s future.

First, the culture and talent here are world-class, the collaboration and engineering caliber are unmatched, especially coming from AWS’s notorious burnout culture. The team is executing, not coasting.

Second, the broader market seems to miss where modern AI actually runs. People talk about third-party models like Claude disrupting Search, but we need to remember where Anthropics cores are physically hosted: Google Cloud. For every consumer query dollar that might shift away from legacy search, a substantial portion gets pushed right back into GCP enterprise spend.

Third, look at the underlying economics. GCP’s 103% YoY acceleration in AI compute isn’t just vanity growth, the margins on AI infrastructure are very favorable. More importantly, these cores creates a massive gravitational drag: when enterprises come for our TPUs and GPUs, they bring their standard compute, high-throughput storage, databases (Spanner, AlloyDB), and analytics (BigQuery) with them. That is exceptionally sticky, high-margin revenue.

Alphabet trading near a 14 P/E (historically cheap) suggests the market is pricing in terminal search decay while ignoring the enterprise cloud engine right in front of them. The sentiment gap is wide, which is exactly why I continue to invest.

Sector Snapshot: Travel Tech Funding Heads Toward Multiyear Low Despite AI Push

📅 2026-10-30  |  Read Source →

Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question.

Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech.

The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count.

AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning.

The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019.

Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.”

Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States.

The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews, which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth, with participation from Atomico, HarbourVest Partners, Kinnevik, Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management. The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion.

Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities, joined by New Alliance Capital, Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely, develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis.

Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue.

Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field, bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million.

Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo, which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital, Isai and Ternel. The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments.

Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities.

Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets, a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February.

On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November.

Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing.
