Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

It was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything. The workings might be different under the hood, depending on the reference boxes, but the syntax and expected outcomes would be same: push to one edge, keep at the center, spread around evenly, etc.

Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?

For example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid. In other words, it reads like a table, but acts like a grid, allowing me to use grid properties. Believe it or not, some form of this was used in the past to make tables responsive.

Before I kill off a table in this article though: there are a lot of advantages to straight-up tables. They provide a clean semantic layout that browsers perfectly understand and translate for assistive technology when needed. There’s even a element.

On the CSS side of things, there are indeed circumstances where CSS Grid is necessary for its intrinsic responsiveness, source order independence, and positioning. That’s why it’s an indispensable tool for layouts. Use that and let HTML tables to do the work of actually displaying tabular data!

But there’s the presentational benefit of table we should consider. Technically,

is not a presentational element like a
. It’s semantic: the browser and I share a common meaning for it. But whether the browser understands it as such or not, if I read
I believe it’s a heading followed by data. Let’s say that’s pseudo-semantic to me, if presentation is not the right term.

That pseudo-semanticism is still useful. It’s the difference between me having to read this:

Despite there being semantic elements for titles, like

and , they don’t bring in the connection that

and have, and it’s better to reserve
and
for textual structuring like glossaries rather than layouts.

this way? I mean, the table itself merely used as pseudo-semantic markup skin:

Then, this CSS and its outcome (for the first markup):

To me, the latter markup example — a pseudo-semantic table — is easier to scan than a handful of generic divs. I get the pseudo-semantics of table, and the ease of using CSS Grid for the layout. As for browsers, none of them have shunned this sort of Frankenstein creation, at least yet. The VoiceOver and keyboard navigation works as if it’s a real table.

But it’s understandable why it looks more than a little gross and against the grain of what we should be able to. We’re encouraged to maintain a separation of concerns between content and presentation and this does exactly that without affecting the tables semantics, such as its role. But maybe it should? There are plenty of other HTML elements that CSS is capable of busting.

The pseudo-semantic angle is what really sold me here. I run an informational niche site that’s full of reference tables (status codes, payment schedules), and scanning raw markup with / pairs is so much easier to read than a pile of nested divs. That said, Mike Mai’s point about VoiceOver gives me pause — I’ll probably keep this trick for decorative layouts and leave the actual data tables semantically intact.

This is a fun experiment, and I especially liked the distinction you drew between a real table and a pseudo-semantic one. Once display: grid is applied, the browser no longer treats the th and td relationship the way it does in a normal table, so the visual connection stays for sighted readers while the structural meaning is lost. That trade-off is what makes Mike Mai’s point land for me: it is convenient for the author, but assistive technology does not get the same benefit. I would keep this pattern for a purely presentational card only where the same information is also available in a straightforward, accessible form, rather than using it for actual data.

The Ongoing Crisis in Menopause Care

📅 2026-10-29  |  Read Source →

Few medical providers are adequately trained to treat menopause, a new study finds, and even fewer understand how hormonal changes aggravate ADHD symptoms.

Suffering through menopausal hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, mood shifts, and memory problems? Wondering why your ADHD medication has suddenly become less effective? Considering a visit with your doctor to better understand and treat these deeply disruptive symptoms?

Sadly, your healthcare provider may be less informed than you might hope.

A disturbing but unsurprising analysis, published recently in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Women’s Health, found that many healthcare professionals are ill-equipped to provide responsive, coordinated, evidence-based treatment and support to help women navigate this often-challenging stage of life. It cited inadequate medical training, paltry research, and persistent gaps in knowledge as reasons for the “fragmented care.”1

The analysis of 89 studies on health system responsiveness across the U.S. and several other countries also found that women in marginalized groups disproportionately experienced barriers to care and received limited information about available treatment options by providers.

A woman who has gone 12 months without a menstrual period is in menopause. The median age for menopause is 51, though many women with ADHD are known to experience the onset earlier.

[Get This Free Download: Menopause and ADHD]

Declining estrogen levels during perimenopause and menopause are associated with reduced dopamine, leading to worsening ADHD symptoms and emotional dysregulation in many women – even those who had previously managed their ADHD symptoms well with medication, according to a separate study published in the Journal of Attention Disorders.

In surveys conducted over recent years, thousands of women have disclosed to ADDitude how midlife hormonal changes exacerbated their ADHD symptoms and adversely affected every area of their lives, from work performance and sleep to relationships with family and friends. Many said they sought help from providers who had limited knowledge and few clinical studies to consult.

“Perimenopause and menopause play a big role in my inattentive ADHD, and I wish more was known by those who diagnose and treat us,” said Cindy, a ADDitude reader from Santa Clara, California.

“The fact that females are massively underdiagnosed and understudies is horrible but not surprising,” said another ADDitude reader who was diagnosed with ADHD at age 38. “How symptoms may change during perimenopause and menopause, how this affects your home life as a wife and mother, is not talked about enough.”

“It’s insane,” said another ADDitude reader, “and nobody is helping us to treat the super storm of symptoms, including brain fog, exhaustion, headaches, and so on.”

Menopausal hormone therapy is considered the most effective treatment for alleviating common symptoms and is often recommended for women experiencing adverse effects of perimenopause. Non-hormonal medications and complementary approaches, including cognitive behavioral therapy, have also shown benefits in symptom management, the Lancet analysis said.

Carole Fleck is Editor-in-Chief at ADDitude magazine.

Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done

📅 2026-10-29  |  Read Source →

More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots.

Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1, the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low.

One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds.

So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data.

The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set.

On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular.

At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals.

Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus, Jeff Bezos’ physical AI startup that launched last year.

Model developer World Labs, led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor.

For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients.

Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group.

So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories.

AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies.

Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed.

Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies.

The First-Time Experiences Kids Will Never Forget in Citrus County

📅 2026-10-28  |  Read Source →

There’s something magical about watching your child experience something for the very first time. The wide eyes. The nervous excitement. The inevitable “Can we do that again?” And the stories they tell anyone who will listen long after you’ve unpacked the suitcases. In Citrus County, Florida, those moments are practically everywhere.

Welcome to Crystal River, Homosassa, Inverness and Floral City—a refreshingly wild side of the Sunshine State where first-time adventures come naturally. Here, kids can swim alongside gentle manatees, search the Gulf for their own dinner, explore underwater worlds and discover that sometimes the best adventures don’t require a screen, a schedule or even a ticket. It’s outdoorsy without requiring your family to be expert adventurers, educational without feeling like school and relaxed enough that you don’t need a vacation from your vacation.

An easy road trip from many Florida cities and an unexpected nature escape for families traveling from farther away, Citrus County is where your next family vacation can become a collection of unforgettable firsts.

Imagine the look on your child’s face when a 1,000-pound manatee glides through the water nearby. It’s the kind of moment that makes even the too-cool-for-everything tween forget to play it cool.

Crystal River is known as the Manatee Capital of the World, and it’s one of the few places in North America where families can swim with these gentle giants in their natural habitat. Book a certified tour with an outfitter like Explorida, where guides teach families the importance of respectful wildlife viewing, including the all-important “Manatee Manners.” Tours operate year-round, but winter is prime time for seeing larger numbers of manatees as they gather in the area’s warm springs.

Not ready to snorkel? Explorida also offers manatee-viewing eco cruises, so younger kids, grandparents and anyone who prefers staying dry can still experience the magic.

Why they’ll remember it: Because seeing a manatee in a book or aquarium is one thing. Sharing the water with one in the wild? That’s a story they’ll be telling for years.

For little explorers (and grandparents) who aren’t ready to jump into the water, the next best thing might be watching nature unfold right beneath their feet.

At Three Sisters Springs, a boardwalk winds around the crystal-clear spring complex, offering an incredible vantage point for spotting manatees during the winter months. The surrounding wetlands are also home to birds and other wildlife, turning an ordinary walk into an impromptu nature safari.

Give your kids a challenge: How many manatees can they spot? Can they find a mother and calf? What other animals can they discover along the way?

It’s stroller-friendly, wonderfully unhurried and proof that you don’t have to get wet to make a splash.

Why they’ll remember it: The thrill of spotting their first wild manatee all on their own, and the pride of being the one who shouts, “I SEE ONE!”

Forget searching for seashells on the beach. In Citrus County, kids can head underwater on a real-life treasure hunt and bring home something delicious.

During summer scalloping season, families venture into the shallow Gulf waters off Crystal River and Homosassa, armed with snorkels, masks and mesh bags, to search the seagrass for bay scallops. Think Easter egg hunt, except underwater. And instead of chocolate, the reward might end up on your dinner plate.

Never tried scalloping? That’s part of the fun. Guided excursions with operators like Explorida help beginners learn the ropes, with equipment, guidance and plenty of encouragement along the way. And the moment your child spots that first scallop hiding in the grass? Pure victory.

Why they’ll remember it: There’s something incredibly satisfying about finding your own food. Just wait until they proudly announce at dinner, “I caught that!”

Tinybeans tip: Scalloping is seasonal, typically July through September. Check current dates, regulations and tour availability before planning your adventure.

For kids who’ve never tried kayaking and paddleboarding, Citrus County offers a pretty spectacular introduction. Imagine pushing off from shore, dipping a paddle into clear spring water and realizing that, for the first time, you’re helping steer the adventure.

At Hunter Springs Park in Crystal River, families will find a freshwater swimming area, kayak launch, waterfront boardwalk, picnic spots and a playground. The spring water stays around 72°F year-round, and during cooler months, there’s even a chance of spotting a manatee.

Bring your own paddle craft or book with a local outfitter. Younger kids can ride along with an adult, while older children can take a more active role in navigating.

The best part? There’s no rush to get anywhere. Stop to watch a bird, look for fish beneath the surface or simply float and take it all in.

Why they’ll remember it: That first feeling of independence. The realization that they can help navigate a kayak, explore somewhere new and discover what’s around the next bend.

What if your kids could explore an underwater world without ever putting on a swimsuit? At Ellie Schiller Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park, they can. The park’s famous Fish Bowl Underwater Observatory lets visitors descend beneath the surface of the spring to watch fish and, when present, manatees swim past the windows. For kids, it’s a little like stepping inside a nature documentary.

Back above water, shady, stroller-accessible boardwalks lead past native Florida wildlife, including black bears, alligators, red wolves and Florida panthers. Daily manatee programs offer another opportunity to learn about these remarkable animals and why protecting their habitat matters.

It’s an ideal first introduction to Florida’s wild side, especially for families with younger children or anyone who prefers wildlife encounters on dry land.

Why they’ll remember it: Because the first time you see the underwater world from a fish’s point of view, you never look at the water quite the same way again.

Remember the first time you rode your bike somewhere that wasn’t your driveway or neighborhood? The freedom. The excitement. The feeling that you could go anywhere? That’s what makes the Withlacoochee State Trail such a great family adventure.

Stretching approximately 47 paved miles through forests, lakes and charming small towns, the trail is flat, scenic and easy to explore in family-sized sections. No one expects your six-year-old to conquer all 47 miles.

Start in downtown Inverness, where the trail passes through the Depot District, and let your kids help choose how far to ride. Along the way, keep an eye out for birds, turtles and other wildlife. When everyone starts asking about snacks, make The Train Station part of your plan for pizza, pretzels and a well-earned break.

Why they’ll remember it: Their first real biking expedition, complete with the satisfaction of going farther than they thought they could. Bonus points if they proudly tell everyone how many miles they conquered.

You can tell your kids mermaids aren’t real. Or you can take them somewhere that might make them question everything.

At Mertailor’s Mermaid Aquarium Encounter in Lecanto, live mermaids perform underwater alongside fish, rays and other marine life, creating a magical experience that feels straight out of a storybook. But there’s more here than mermaid magic. The indoor aquarium features over 20 exhibits, interactive touch tanks, sharks, stingrays and freshwater animals, giving curious kids plenty to explore.

For children ages nine and up, the separate Discover Mermaid experience takes things a step further, with the chance to put on a mermaid tail and monofin and learn to swim like one. It’s also a great rainy-day adventure or a welcome break from the Florida sunshine.

Why they’ll remember it: Because watching a mermaid swim with sharks is pretty unforgettable. But getting to be a mermaid for the first time? That’s next-level vacation bragging rights.

Not every unforgettable first requires an adrenaline rush. Sometimes it’s the first time your kids experience what it feels like to slow down.

Head to Homosassa for a waterfront meal at Crumps’ Landing, where palm trees, water views and laid-back Florida charm set the scene for a different kind of family dinner. No rushing to make a reservation across town. No squeezing in one more attraction. Just good food, waterfront views and time to talk about everything you’ve done together. Let the kids recap their favorite adventures while you watch the sky change colors over the water.

Why they’ll remember it: It may not be the meal they remember years from now, but they’ll remember the feeling: salty air, sunset skies and everyone together with nowhere else they need to be.

Remember when simply staying in a hotel felt like the most exciting thing in the world? Now imagine staying somewhere that puts you right in the middle of the action.

Paddletail Waterfront Lodge sits on King’s Bay in Crystal River, giving families easy access to the area’s most memorable experiences. With paddlecraft activities, manatee excursions, waterfront dining, a pool and complimentary hot breakfast, the lodge makes it easy to spend less time coordinating logistics and more time having fun. Rooms with refrigerators and microwaves, and select kitchenette options also make traveling with kids a little easier.

Wake up knowing that another adventure is waiting just outside.

Why they’ll remember it: Because when the place you stay is part of the experience, even the moments between activities become vacation memories.

Here’s a first that might surprise you: What if you gave your kids an entire afternoon to decide what the family does? No packed itinerary. No racing from one attraction to another. No pressure to squeeze every last minute out of your vacation.

One of the best things about Citrus County is that it gives families room to explore at their own pace. Maybe your kids want another swim at Hunter Springs. Maybe they want to wander downtown Crystal River, go for another bike ride, find ice cream or sit by the water and watch for wildlife. Let them choose.

Because sometimes the most meaningful first isn’t swimming with a manatee or spotting a scallop. It’s the first time your child discovers that an adventure doesn’t need to be planned to be unforgettable.

Why they’ll remember it: Because they helped create the memory themselves. And those are often the moments that stick.

Someday, your kids might forget what they packed, what they ate for breakfast or how long the drive took. But they’ll remember the first manatee they saw. The first scallop they found. The first time they paddled across a spring or rode their bike farther than ever before. And you’ll remember the look on their faces when they did.

That’s the magic of Citrus County. It’s not just a place to visit. It’s a place to try something new, discover something extraordinary and make the kinds of memories that grow more meaningful with time.

Ready to make some first-time memories? Plan your Crystal River and Citrus County getaway and request a FREE Visitor Guide, or book a certified manatee tour and get ready for an adventure your family won’t soon forget.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

📅 2026-10-28  |  Read Source →

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service

📅 2026-10-28  |  Read Source →

A model can reason about a task. Completing that task takes more: the right context, tools, execution environment, and controls, and an agent loop that brings them together.

Microsoft’s unified harness strategy brings a shared execution foundation across our agent experiences while preserving customer choice. In Microsoft Foundry, that means you can choose a supported model and decide how much of the agent stack to build yourself, without having to assemble every layer around it.

Today, we’re introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service in public preview. It gives developers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. It’s our opinionated approach to helping agents complete complex work. We’re also announcing general availability of long-running resilience for hosted agents. Together, these capabilities help developers build more reliable agents for complex, long-running workflows.

Many teams building agents end up implementing the same execution machinery: coordinating model and tool calls, maintaining working context, managing files, and deciding how to continue when a task requires more than one step. That work matters, but it isn’t usually what differentiates your application.

The Copilot harness gives you a managed execution system for agents you define declaratively in Foundry Agent Service. Microsoft runs the agent loop and sandbox; you bring the knowledge, procedures, and tools that make the agent yours.

The public preview brings together four building blocks:

The harness manages working context as tasks develop and coordinates model and tool steps toward a requested outcome, within configured limits and policy boundaries. You choose a supported Foundry model without having to rewrite the orchestration around it.

That lets your team focus on improving the agent’s expertise and evaluating its results.

“With the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service, we had a solution running in less than a week, allowing us to focus on design and capabilities instead of the infrastructure underneath it. That speed will help us bring our vision of AI that runs within and alongside our products to market faster.”

— Chris Evans, Chief Technology Officer, Confluence Technologies

“The Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service gives Fashable a powerful foundation for turning complex sourcing processes into governed, measurable agent workflows. We see the opportunity to generate complete tech packs from our knowledge and templates, while extending our A2A sourcing network beyond digitally connected suppliers through email and voice. Most importantly, we can equip brand and manufacturer agents with deeper knowledge and new capabilities to work across sourcing and negotiation without automating away accountability: agents can discover, engage and calculate, while commercially binding decisions remain under human control.”

Consider an agent that researches a topic, analyzes supporting data, and produces an evidence-backed brief. The same pattern can support market research, operational analysis, or an internal planning workflow: instructions define the outcome, skills define the method, and tools provide access to evidence.

Here’s a compact example using the preview Azure Developer CLI (azd) surface.

First, put a reusable procedure in skills/research-brief/SKILL.md:

Then describe the skill and agent in azure.yaml:

Set the referenced environment values, then deploy and invoke:

azd is one authoring option. You can also start in the Foundry portal or use Foundry Toolkit for Visual Studio Code. In the GitHub Copilot app, the Microsoft Foundry plugin and Microsoft Foundry Skill provide a conversational path to creating and managing prompt agents.

These options let you build on a managed harness. When your application needs a different framework or its own execution logic, hosted agents give you another path.

Hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service let you bring your own framework, agent loop, middleware, dependencies, and runtime behavior while Foundry manages hosting. Long-running resilience for hosted agents is generally available this week, helping agents recover from interruptions during work that takes hours or days.

Foundry detects interruptions and restarts the work with its original input. Your code saves progress and intermediate results so the agent can pick up where it left off. If the agent updates another system, your workflow also needs to prevent duplicate actions when work restarts.

For example, an agent analyzing a large dataset can save completed stages and resume from the last checkpoint. If it also creates a report in another system, it should check whether the report already exists before creating it again.

Foundry provides the recovery foundation; your application determines what to save and how to resume. Conversation history alone isn’t enough to restore work in progress.

These workflows have different requirements, and there isn’t one right level of abstraction for every agent. Foundry Agent Service lets you choose where to invest your engineering effort:

Start with the level that fits your application’s requirements, rather than taking ownership of infrastructure you don’t need to differentiate.

During this preview, select the Microsoft Copilot harness when creating the agent. Existing agents are unchanged, switching the harness after creation isn’t supported yet, and Foundry manages the execution environment’s CPU, memory, and idle settings.

You can start in the Microsoft Foundry portal or use azd to keep the agent definition alongside the rest of your application.

Pricing: Billing for the Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service begins December 1, 2026, with consumption-based pricing. Harness runtime usage is free before December 1; model inference and separately billed tools and connected services remain subject to their applicable charges. Starting December 1, sandbox compute and memory are billed at USD $0.0994 per vCPU-hour and $0.0118 per GiB-hour, respectively. Prices may vary by region and agreement.

Jeff Hollan is the VP of Product for the Microsoft Foundry Agent Platform.

Viswajeeet is a Principal Software Engineer on Foundry Agents Team in CoreAI, where he leads managed agents platform. He also works on agent identity and toolboxes in Foundry to help customers’ agents achieve better outcomes with right set of controls.

Anthony is a product manager on the Microsoft Foundry team, focused on helping developers build and run AI agents. He works on Foundry Agent Service, making powerful agent capabilities easier to use without the overhead of managing the underlying infrastructure.

6 ways to make homework less of a battle when your kid has ADHD

📅 2026-10-28  |  Read Source →

Home / Health & Wellness / Children's Health

A child psychiatrist on getting through the after-school hours without a standoff.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 28, 2026

Tonight’s homework is a single worksheet. It’s been 50 minutes. Your kid has sharpened every pencil in the house, visited the bathroom twice, and is now face-down on the floor insisting it’s impossible. You can feel your patience slipping by the second.

If homework battles turn your evenings into a standoff, you’re far from alone, especially if your child has ADHD. About 1 in 9 US kids have been diagnosed with the condition , and the American Academy of Pediatrics says it can profoundly affect a child’s academic achievement. For families managing ADHD, the after-school stretch is often the hardest part of the day.

There’s a reason those hours are so trying. By the time a child with ADHD gets home,  they’ve spent “six or seven hours working harder than their classmates to sit still and focus,” says Michael Morse, MD, a board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrist who directs the ADHD & Anxiety Center at Alvord Baker and is an associate professor of psychiatry at Georgetown University. That effort is used up, and for many kids the medication has worn off too, so “the after-school brain is often a tired brain.”

The resistance usually isn’t a matter of defiance. Executive function, the set of skills needed for getting started, planning and keeping track of steps, develops more slowly in kids with ADHD. That’s why a child can freeze in front of an assignment they’re fully capable of completing, and why the thing that helps is making the first step smaller rather than pushing harder.

The worst time to start homework is the moment your child walks through the door. The school day has already drained the same systems homework demands, so Morse suggests framing the immediate after-school window as a time to refuel. “A snack with some protein comes first, because after-school hunger makes both focus and mood worse,” he says. Movement comes next, whether that’s riding a bike or walking the dog, which burns off the day’s tension and helps many kids with ADHD settle. Make the break predictable with a clear end, and pick a consistent homework time that comes after the break and well before your child is too fried to think.

Most importantly, hold off on screens. “The transition from screens to homework can be particularly painful,” Morse says, so it’s usually easier not to turn them on after school at all.

“A task feels too big when a child can’t see where it starts,” Morse says. Many kids with ADHD freeze in front of a big assignment because their brain can’t break it into steps on its own, so the task is to shrink the first step until it feels easy.

Say a book report is due in two weeks. Sit down together and have your child break it into pieces: choose the book, read one chapter, jot notes on the main character. Then put each piece on a calendar so the deadline isn’t, in Morse’s words, “a cliff at the end.” For a single night’s work, 10 math problems can become two sets of five with a break in between. And when your child finishes a piece, say so out loud, since that small win makes the next one easier to start. (Younger kids need the pieces smaller and the check-ins more frequent.)

“Players usually appreciate coaches who run laps with them,” Morse says. He encourages parents to be “a coach and a model, not an enforcer.” In practice that can look like sitting at the kitchen table with your own work, while your child does theirs. A calm adult nearby helps many kids with ADHD get started and keep going. What a coach doesn’t do is finish the work so it comes back perfect, “because then the teacher never sees what the child can really do,” Morse says. The job is to help plan the night and praise the effort while leaving the outcome up to your child.

When homework turns into a power struggle, handing a little control back to your child can often defuse it. Offer two options you’re happy with either way, like “Math or reading first?” or “Before dinner or after, but before screens.” “A choice gives a child some control,” Morse says, which can take the fight out of the room before it starts. (If homework is still a daily battle no matter what you try, Morse notes a tutor can often take the coaching role with less friction than a parent.)

Some nights, the right move is to stop. “A parent should call it when the homework is no longer teaching anything or when substantial conflict emerges,” Morse says. If your child is in tears, exhausted or stuck on the same problem despite your help, more pushing won’t produce learning. “It mostly produces a worse night and a child who dreads the next one,” he says. When you stop, have your child’s back by sending the teacher a short note about how long they worked and where they got stuck. Most teachers would rather know.

“Your relationship with your child is more important than any assignment,” Morse says, and that relationship is what carries a kid through years of school. Kids with ADHD already hear a lot of criticism, and “if homework turns every evening into a battle, home stops feeling like the place where they’re accepted.”

Some homework problems are too big to solve at the kitchen table. “I’d start advocating when the problem looks bigger than effort,” Morse says. Watch for homework that routinely takes far longer than the teacher intended, work your child understands but can’t get written down or turned in, or nights that keep ending in tears. Those point to a gap between what the assignment asks and what your child can do right now, and pushing harder at home won’t close it.

Start by telling the teacher how long the work is actually taking. Some kids need more formal support through a 504 plan or an individualized education program, the school plans that put accommodations in writing. This matters especially for girls, Morse says, “whose late-night effort can keep their grades up and hide how much they’re struggling.”

As kids get older, Morse’s advice is to hand over the wheel gradually, with middle school as the moment to watch, when additional teachers and long-term projects arrive just as parents tend to step back. Teach your child to use a planner, check in briefly each evening, and let them take on more as they show they can. The long-term goal is teaching a kid which tasks will always need a system or a helper, because “knowing when to ask for help is one of the most valuable skills a teenager can carry into adult life.”

That need goes well beyond ADHD. Accountability partners and body doubles, “people whose quiet company helps you start and stay on task,” work for nearly everyone. “Not everyone knows to ask,” Morse says.

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

Ten years later, I still grieve my miscarriage

📅 2026-10-28  |  Read Source →

Home / Getting Pregnant / Miscarriage & Loss

When I lost my baby, I knew it was a day I’d never forget. And then I did.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Oct. 28, 2026

Content warning: Discussion of pregnancy loss ahead.

I was cleaning my kitchen, pop music blaring from a speaker, when I glanced at the digital calendar on my counter. That’s when I saw it—the butterfly emoji that flutters every August 21 to memorialize the day I lost my pregnancy.

I was gutted. But this time it wasn’t because of the miscarriage. It was because I forgot. For the first time in 10 years, the date my baby’s heart stopped beating had slipped my mind.

It’s not hard for me to bring myself back to that day. At my 12-week appointment, the doctor ran a fetal doppler across my belly, searching for a heartbeat she would never find. I watched the crease between her eyebrows deepen as she moved the wand around. She tried to reassure me there could be a reason she couldn’t find the heartbeat. Still, it made sense to get an ultrasound.

I headed off to a new location. I didn’t call anyone, doing my best to will “it’s fine” into existence. I sat nervously in the waiting room, tapping my leg up and down as I listened for my name.

When it was my turn, I laid back on the table, prepped for the squeeze of cool jelly on my stomach, then watched a screen on the wall as the ultrasound tech poked around to find my baby.

And there it was. The makings of my second born lit up on the screen. Those images are always a bit tough to discern, but I could clearly see a head, a body, and four limbs. But those limbs weren’t moving, and the tech stayed quiet. She pressed buttons, took snapshots, and kept her gaze trained squarely on her computer screen. When she finished, she said, “The doctor will be in to talk to you,” then scurried out the door.

Seconds later someone else popped in and asked me to follow them to another room. I now realize I was taking up precious space near the ultrasound equipment. They’d need it for their next appointment, and the news I was about to hear might stun me in place for some time.

The moment is crystal clear in my memory even ten years later. I remember the hard plastic chair I sat in. I remember looking around the room and realizing that half of it was used for storage. There were boxes of papers and remnants of mailers alongside random supplies waiting for their real homes. Next to me, a box of tissues sat on a small table.

When the doctor walked in, he introduced himself. I don’t remember his name, but I’ll never forget his somber look when he said, “It’s not good news.” The floor falling out from beneath me. I called my husband in tears, barely able to say, “There’s no heartbeat,” then made a desperate call to my mom to share the same news.

I don’t remember how I got back to my grandmother’s house, where she was watching my 2-year-old son. I know I drove there, but the memory is hazy, overlaid with the sadness, terror and anxiety that were coursing through me.

When I arrived, I collapsed into my grandmother’s arms. “They couldn’t find a heartbeat,” I said, fighting back tears as my son watched us intently. She tightened her grip on me and let me dissolve.

I suffered a missed miscarriage—my body didn’t recognize that the baby growing inside had died. But based on its size and development, doctors were able to tell me that the heart likely stopped beating at 10.5 weeks. That’s how I came to mark August 21 as the day my baby died.

In the years that followed, I anxiously awaited both that date and my due date as they crept closer. I knew they would be hard. Over the first couple of years, I’d plan for unproductive days, knowing I’d fall back into my grief. I’d spend the morning each August 21 remembering the day I found out, going over every detail as I let the tears rain down. I’d search for signs of butterflies, which became a hopeful symbol to me in the wake of my miscarriage.

But ten years later, I was caught up in the details of a very busy life. I’m a working mom with two school-aged kids who spends much of my time chauffeuring them between playdates and sports practices.

It’s likely a good sign that August 21 no longer looms over me like a dark cloud. In those early years of letting the grief wash over me in full force, I gave my mind, body and heart the space to release its tension and ache. But forgetting the date brought its own type of grief. It was a reminder of how far I’ve come, and how far my baby never did.

Ten years later, I still grieve my miscarriage, but that grief has evolved. I will always wonder what that little life would have become, and why they weren’t given the chance. I will always take a moment to pause and remember the hope, joy and love I felt in the early weeks of that pregnancy, even if I need the calendar to remind me to do so.

And most importantly, I will always talk about it. With time, grief has lessened its stranglehold on my heart and emotions. What remains of my grief is more like a tool. It appears when I need to be a supporter. It boosts my voice so I can help others in the throes of their own despair.

One in 4 women will experience pregnancy or infant loss in their lifetime. I’m a 1-in-4, and I hope sharing my story helps someone else feel less alone in their pain, no matter where she is on her grieving journey.

October is Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month. If you or someone you know is struggling with a postpartum mental health challenge after a pregnancy or infant loss, call the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-9-HELP4MOMS (1-800-943-5746). This free, confidential service provides access to trained counselors and resources 24 hours a day, 7 days a week in English, Spanish, and more than 60 other languages. They can offer support and information related to before, during, and after pregnancy.

Today, we laid out our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive, end-to-end software delivery system in the world.

Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters.

Today at GitHub Universe, we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it.

The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better.

This agentic software delivery system solves for three things:

GitHub is built for developers and their agents. We’re also making the underlying primitives available, so you can build your own bespoke solutions. You stay in control of the work, the tools, and the cost.

Today at Universe, we showed some of the latest products and features in action, starting with the GitHub Copilot app.

The GitHub Copilot app is designed from the ground up for agentic software delivery. It connects your agents and tools across projects, so you can direct the work without making every handoff. And it’s for more than producing code: you can write specs, present design discussions, or analyze telemetry in one agent-first surface.

Different tasks need different models. Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task.

Available natively in the GitHub Copilot app starting today, Copilot projects let you run agent work across multiple repos in fully managed, parallel sessions. You have one place to track progress, make decisions, and direct what happens next. That means you can spend less time managing execution and more time deciding what’s worth building.

Your work shouldn’t restart when you switch devices or tools. Session continuity lets you start and follow the same cloud agent session across the GitHub app, VS Code, the CLI, and the web. Start from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check in on it from github.com at lunch. The agent keeps working in the cloud. Our multi-model harness that enables it is powerful, fast, and cost-efficient.

Copilot automations let you create AI-powered workflows within your repo. They run in the cloud, and you can kick them off manually or set them up to respond to an event or run on a schedule. That lets you coordinate agents to handle tasks such as issue triage and code review. And now, automations can learn from their outcomes and propose improvements for you to review and approve. That’s the learning engine in practice. Use the results of the completed work to make the next run better.

More code means more pull requests and more demand for review. Moving faster only helps if we can maintain the quality of what ships. Copilot code review surfaces meaningful, actionable bugs that developers need to catch. Today, we introduced Copilot code review Max, which posted the highest F1 score on ReviewBench for high-severity issues. Lite and Balanced keep everyday reviews fast; the new Max provides a deeper look when a change needs it.

Starting today, GitHub Enterprise customers can use all Copilot features without buying a separate subscription. That includes GitHub Copilot app, code review, automations, and more. You pay for the AI credits you use.

This is available through GitHub Sales today, with self-serve coming soon. Existing Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise customers can keep their current plans or move over when they’re ready. GitHub also remains open and extensible. Keep using the tools your team depends on, including Cloudflare, Datadog, Figma, and more.

All of this depends on a foundation that’s fast, reliable, and built to scale. Agents are changing the volume and shape of software development. Adding capacity matters, but capacity alone won’t get us there. We’ve also had to change the architecture.

We’re also migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure, while continuing to serve incredible levels of traffic from developers around the world. We expect to complete the migration early next year. Those investments give us more room to grow. The next step is building the systems that handle the work.

We’ve scaled Git for years as activity on GitHub has grown. The agentic era calls for a different ceiling on throughput and reliability. Three principles guide our new Git architecture: simplify the primitives, decouple storage from compute, and minimize coordination.

Git’s just one example of the work we’re doing to scale the platform. We’ve done a lot of work across GitHub’s AI gateway, the harness, and much more.

Our jobs are changing, but developers are more important than ever. I think all the software we’ve written to date will amount to less than 1% of the software we’ll write in the next five years. The opportunity isn’t just to produce more code. It’s to solve problems we couldn’t solve before.

That’s why we’re connecting the full software delivery system, giving developers better ways to work with agents, and evolving the infrastructure for what comes next. And we’re doing it on GitHub, where we can build together.

Jay Parikh is a seasoned executive, board member, and advisor to some of the world’s fastest growing and most successful consumer, developer, and enterprise technology companies. As Executive Vice President of CoreAI at Microsoft, Parikh leads the organization building the end-to-end agentic system required to build, ship, and run AI agents in the Enterprise. His teams, including GitHub, also build the tools and platforms developers need to create the next generation of software.

Previously, Parikh was CEO of a cloud security startup and, before that, was Facebook’s global head of engineering and infrastructure. For more than a decade, he led the teams that built and operated the physical infrastructure and software that supported the company’s growth from 300 million people to more than 3 billion. His teams worked across the stack, from data centers, servers, and subsea cables to software, data, AI, and security systems. Through leadership roles in the Open Compute Project and Telecom Infra Project, he helped extend infrastructure innovation beyond a single company to benefit entire industries.

Earlier in his career, Parikh held leadership roles at Akamai and Ning. He brings a systems thinker’s perspective to a deeply human challenge: how to build teams that keep learning, moving, and delivering as the world changes around them.

See how a record year of growth reached every industry, every field, and every kind of builder in the 2026 Octoverse report.

Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined.

Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati, a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft, and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers. Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before.

That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture.

Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most:

Underneath it all, AI models and the harnesses built around them have advanced over the past year, and developers have more to choose from. Growth is moving quickly: one year into last year’s five-year developer growth projections, every country we projected has already closed at least a fifth of its distance to 2030, and our own forecasting models no longer agree on where it will go next.

This year was all about momentum. Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day.

Agents were one of the tools developers leaned on hardest this year, pulling them deeper into daily work. Among repos created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one, sign that individuals and teams building with agents from day one are moving at a markedly different pace.

Developers also relied on automations to keep projects moving. GitHub Actions ran a job 1,440 times every second this year. This equals 124 million times a day and is more than three times last year’s total. Developers merged more than 30 million Dependabot pull requests to keep dependencies current and reduce the use of known vulnerabilities, about double 2025’s pace.

Our telemetry shows activity climbing steadily from January, then surging around June, as if developers everywhere saw new possibilities at once. Right around then, a cluster of industry-wide shifts landed: better underlying models, the harnesses and tools built around them, and the agents running on both. Agents moved from single-session tools to persistent ones that could track progress across days and orchestrate other specialized agents. Just as important, agents began making extensive use of the cloud, executing work remotely as well as on local machines.

This momentum is showing up both in brand-new repos and from developers who have been building for years. From June onwards, about 55% of all commits came from brand new repositories. But plenty more commits came from developers who’ve been around a while: developers who pushed code in the past 12 months have been on GitHub for an average of 36 months, and of those who opened a pull request in August, more than 75% pushed code in September. They are also branching out: the average developer now works across 10% more repositories than they did a year ago.

That staying power shows up in open source too. Public contributions soared to 2.5 billion in 2026, more than double last year’s total (1.12 billion). Behind those numbers are developers who keep showing up, like @kinlane, who made more than 1 million contributions across his public repositories using agentic workflows to keep a machine-readable catalog of public API information current. Another example is @kim-em, who made more than 178,000 contributions while maintaining mathlib, which is a community library of computer-checked mathematics. @andig, a maintainer of the open source EV charging controller and home energy management system evcc, contributed over 21,000 times.

These are just a few examples of the work millions of developers do every day. To all the developers doing work like this and beyond: we see you, and we’re glad you’re building.

Behind every number in this report is a developer. GitHub now serves more than 225 million of them, and the community is growing around the globe. The United States (38.3 million) and India (32 million) remain the two largest developer communities, and each added more than 10 million developers this year. Brazil added 3.28 million developers on GitHub this year, the third most of any country.

Last year, we projected that India would reach 57.5 million developers by 2030 and the United States 54.7 million. One year into that five-year window, every country in our projections has already closed at least a fifth of the distance to its own 2030 figure. The United States has closed 38.6%, and India 28.3%.

The same momentum shows up across regions, each with its own local context:

One year in, growth is strong against last year’s projection, and projecting the next five years is getting harder. We ran more than 40 forecasting models forward to 2031, time-series and regression models built on historical sign-up and usage data, each assuming a different pace of growth. About half call for “extreme” growth, with developer counts on GitHub more than tripling by 2031. Just under half call for “substantial” growth, doubling to tripling. Only three models expect anything close to modest, under 2x growth.

Forecasts are estimates, and a spread this wide shows how much the 2026 surge widened what is plausible by 2031. What holds steady is the shape of the trend: a developer community growing in more places at once.

In past reports, “everywhere” meant more developers and more countries, such as in the context of the top countries contributing code to public repositories:

This year, it also means more fields, including industries we haven’t measured before.

We’re sharing our view of public repositories by industry using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), which sorts economic activity into sectors. A language model classified random samples of public repositories created each year from 2022 to 2026, assigning each to the industry it serves based on its name, description, topics, and README. We also tracked two signals: whether a repository mentions AI, and whether an agent opened a pull request against it.

The two signals do not always move together. In administrative and support services, mining, health care, and agriculture, more than four in 10 repositories mention AI, yet agent-opened pull requests are rare, less than 3 percent. Construction breaks that pattern. About a quarter of its repositories mention AI, but about 9 percent have agent-opened pull requests, the highest share of any sector, with manufacturing next.

The same classification shows how each industry’s footprint has shifted since 2022, and sectors well beyond software are climbing. Professional, scientific, and technical services rose from fourth to second place among all industries, behind only information. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting climbed two spots, and finance and insurance and health care and social assistance each moved up one. Against each sector’s own 2022 baseline, mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction grew roughly 65 times from a small starting base, administrative and support services and construction 17 to 18 times, and even manufacturing, the slowest of these, almost tripled.

Behind these sector shifts are people who know their fields, now using AI coding agents to build. For example, in manufacturing, a small team built a way to turn a photo of your tools into a custom-fit, 3D-printable drawer organizer. A research lab in health care made it easier for scientists to analyze huge digital scans of tissue samples, the kind pathologists study to understand disease. In Copenhagen, a university lab built a pipeline that classifies video of chickens at play, from frolicking to worm chasing. A University of Waikato energy center built a toolkit that helps industrial plants find heat they can reuse, and Bulgaria’s digital ministry open-sourced a portal where anyone can trace who won a public contract and for how much. For writers, a novelist built a free app that makes a manuscript look like a book as you type. In field after field, the people closest to the problem are building the solution, with agents helping along the way.

Professional, scientific, and technical services, which grew about 5 times over its own 2022 baseline and climbed to second place, is the work of researching, engineering, and advising, and open code has long been part of how that work gets done. In biochemistry, the work behind AlphaFold earned Demis Hassabis and John Jumper a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In computer science, Tensor2Tensor accompanied the paper that introduced the Transformer, the architecture behind today’s large language models, “Attention Is All You Need.” In medicine, sars-cov-2-stability held the code and data behind one of the earliest papers on how long the virus survives in the air and on surfaces. In physics, eht-imaging was one of two open-source libraries used to reconstruct the first image of a black hole. A repository has quietly become part of the paper trail behind published research.

More developers now begin a pull request by specifying what they want and orchestrating the agents that carry it out. By September 2026, more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub started with an agent’s first draft, up from 17% in March. That is 110 million in September alone, about 6x March’s volume.

Agent-started pull requests also more often change multiple files: about 87%, compared with 79% of pull requests without detected agent involvement. They are landing quickly too. In February, 83% of agent-involved pull requests merged within two weeks, a touch behind the roughly 86% for pull requests without detected agent involvement. By September, agent pull requests were at 90%, while the comparison group held at about 86%.

Among GitHub Copilot’s monthly active users, 55% now use agentic features, up from 35% a year ago. The steepest growth is in the most hands-off mode. Copilot cloud agent, where a developer assigns a task and an agent works on it independently, grew 230% year over year, against 85% for agent chat. Developers still ask agents questions, and increasingly they hand over whole tasks.

The willingness to delegate is reflected by the kinds of tasks developers are attempting. Public repositories mentioning interoperability or reverse engineering increased more than 300% year over year, from about 30,000 created in 2025 to more than 130,000 in 2026.

Review is where developers shape what comes back, and more tooling is being built for it. Stacked pull requests, which split related work into smaller changes that are easier to review in sequence, launched as a preview on July 30, and more than 264,000 developers had used them by September. Usage of AI-assisted code review and GitHub Advanced Security both grew more than 90% year over year. The platform also helps secure that work: push protection, which screens for exposed secrets such as API keys and passwords, ran 5.8 billion scans this year, nearly four times 2025’s pace. Developers are investing in how they review code.

Developers match models to the work they hand to their agents. In September 2026, 61% of GitHub Copilot users who selected a model themselves used more than one model across their sessions, up from 50% four months earlier.

The lineup is growing too: developers on paid GitHub Copilot plans used 29 distinct models in May and 47 in September, and no single model carried more than 25% of requests that month. Some model decisions come down to cost and familiarity. Developers weigh price and functionality against need and may lean toward providers they already trust.

To see how developer choices spread, we grouped the models used in GitHub Copilot by what they are built for: deep reasoning and planning, general purpose, and fast and lightweight. We then looked at where requests went, counting only activity where a developer explicitly selected a model. That leaves out cases where GitHub Copilot picks the model (auto model selection), GitHub and Microsoft staff usage, background utility models, duplicate requests used for monitoring and testing, and requests made with a developer’s own API key.

We found that out of every 100 developer-selected requests, 38 went to general purpose models, 37 to deep reasoning and planning models, and 25 to fast and lightweight models. Developers spread their choices across models and functionality, and about 25% of requests go to a fast model.

To see how those choices shift, we looked at them as a time series over the past three months, tracking request share alongside how many developers tried each model and how many kept coming back. Three patterns stand out:

Taken together, the spread across kinds of models points to a lot of choosing: a lineup that keeps growing, a best fit that shifts from one task to the next, and all three kinds of models held in rotation. Many developers also let GitHub Copilot do some of it. In September 2026, 63% of paying GitHub Copilot developers used auto model selection at least once, letting Copilot pick the model for the task.

Planning, implementing, and checking a change each place different demands on a model, in capability, speed, and cost. Project HydraFusion, began as a research preview of model orchestration, matching models to each step of that work. In the CLI and the GitHub Copilot app, it routed almost 60,000 sessions. That work is now generally available as GitHub Copilot Fusion, which brings model orchestration together with auto model selection and chooses the right model for each step behind the scenes.

Language choice has long reflected what developers want to build, what their teams know, and what existing systems require. This year’s data raises the question of whether a fourth influence is emerging: the language an agent picks when a developer doesn’t specify one.

Last year, we reported that TypeScript had overtaken Python and JavaScript to become the most used language on GitHub by contributors. That order held in 2026, with TypeScript first, Python second, and JavaScript third. The pace picked up. From September 2025 to September 2026, TypeScript added 3.62 million monthly contributors, Python 3.23 million, and JavaScript 1.82 million, the largest gains among the top 10 languages. Rust grew fastest by percentage among the top languages, doubling in the past year.

Our forecasts extend recent trends: TypeScript and Python near 13 million monthly contributors each by September 2027, JavaScript at 7.4 million, and every other language in the top 10 below about 2.2 million.

The languages growing fastest are also where AI shows up most. We charted each language’s community growth over the past year against the share of its merged pull requests with detected AI involvement, with bubbles roughly sized to show the size of each language’s community. TypeScript, Python, and Rust, the fastest-growing communities, have the highest shares, about 40% to 44% of merged pull requests. Java, C#, and C++ sit lower, between about 21% and 34%, though AI shows up in more than one in five merged pull requests in every language shown.

The repository data adds another angle. Among repositories created in 2026, TypeScript was the primary language in 35% of those with an observed agent signal, compared to 24% without one. For repositories created before 2026, the gap was similar: 27% with an agent signal, versus 17% without. That suggests developers who work with agents gravitate toward languages where agent output is easier to check. Developers who know exactly what they want still specify the language. But when they leave the choice open, agents appear to favor a narrower set of languages, TypeScript chief among them.

This year, we split the fastest-growing and most-engaged projects on GitHub into two groups: community and independent repositories, and single-vendor or product-led ones. Community and independent projects are foundation-governed, broadly maintained, or led by an individual without a clear commercial sponsor. Single-vendor and product-led projects are open source or source-available and often take substantial community contributions, but strategic control sits with one company.

Read together, the two lists show a division of labor. The community side is mostly the foundation underneath everything else: inference engines like vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp, frameworks like PyTorch, languages and runtimes like Rust and CPython, and platforms like Home Assistant and Godot. The vendor side is mostly the tools developers work with directly: coding agents, editors, and the orchestration around them. Contributors are showing up for both layers. The growth list also includes places built to welcome newcomers, like first-contributions and is-a-dev/register, where many developers make their first pull request.

As part of our research this year, we also tracked the emoji developers used most in their repositories. Across every industry we looked at, the rocket 🚀 topped the list, by a wide margin. A fitting symbol for a year of momentum. Developers on GitHub covered more ground this year: more code, more countries, and more industries than we’ve ever measured. None of that activity changes who decides what the code should do. Someone still has to come up with the idea, whether it’s software that assesses earthquake risk, an open record of how online services change their terms and privacy policies, or an agent skill that makes an AI answer like a caveman to save on words. And someone still has to decide whether it works, whether it belongs, and whether it’s good.

What did change is how much easier it is to take an idea from a weekend thought to something real.

The tools will keep changing, and new industries will keep showing up in places we didn’t expect. What a developer chooses to build, and who they build it for, is still theirs to decide. Rocket emoji and all.

The Joy of Feeling Small

📅 2026-10-28  |  Read Source →

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Awe doesn't always make us feel bigger or better about ourselves. Sometimes it reminds us of our "small self." We see that we’re part of something bigger—and that can be a relief.

Tap, tap, tap. I’m typing away in a café in North London. Outside, the sky is grey. Around me, people are ordering drinks, looking at their phones and talking through problems with colleagues. There must be about twenty of us in here, each with something on our minds.

I have my own concerns. There’s a pile of admin waiting for me, and I’m not especially keen to get on with it.

I stop typing and look around. Each person has a life as complicated as mine. Someone might be worrying about money. Someone else might be looking forward to seeing a friend. A person across the room could have received wonderful news this morning, while somebody else might be quietly dealing with something awful. We sit alongside one another, sharing the same small space, with no real idea what’s happening in each other’s lives.
